newsitem.title: RUSSIA: "Galoshes" perish in Russia's sexual revolution.
newsitem.headline: "Galoshes" perish in Russia's sexual revolution.

text.p: Nicknamed "galoshes", they were partly responsible for the widespread use of abortion as a form of birth control in Russia under communist rule.
Now the thick rubber condoms once referred to as "Product Number One" by prudish Soviet authorities have perished.
The Bakovka Rubber Factory outside Moscow, which once supplied half the condoms for the Soviet Union, is closed for repairs.
When it reopens next year, the factory says, the quality of its output will be unrecognisable from Soviet days.
"We are modernising," said Nikolai Anosov, the factory's chief engineer.
Market reforms have opened Russia up to a flood of cheap, Asian-made condoms which have slowly begun to change attitudes in Russia.
"You can see the results already," said Anosov. "We have reached a world standard and have certificates, not just Russian but international."
In the past, people often bought the condoms only because there was nothing better -- the woman's contraceptive pill was hardly used at all.
Condoms often got put to other uses.
"Tape recorders used to have elastic bands in them. You couldn't buy spare parts so people used to use condoms instead," said Nikolai, 29, who grew up near the factory.
He and his friends would climb through the fence and steal boxes of condoms lying around in the yard to fill with water and throw at people.
"The fence was full of holes," he said. "The condoms were sometimes faulty, too."
At peak production, the factory turned out 200 million condoms a year -- a tiny output considering it was supposed to cover half the need of the Soviet Union which had a population of 250 million.
"Some years we had repairs and then we produced 100 million or none at all," said Anosov.
Now, he says, the factory sells "up to 30 million a year, roughly speaking".
The spread of AIDS and other sexually transmitted diseases has increased the urgency for Russians to overcome the psychological barriers associated with condom use.
"Before, the word condom was seen as a swearword," said Sergei Korotonozhkin, head of the Moscow office of the British condom manufacturer Parma Medical.

His company distributes Playboy condoms in Russia and has now started producing a specific brand aimed at the Russian market at a price more than three times cheaper than the American condoms, which are marketed here as a luxury product.
The new brand is designed to get around the embarrasment associated with condoms in the past.
"To avoid that element, that it was an unacceptable word for the population, we've taken an image from folklore," he said.
The condom looks normal but is named after a popular children's toy called a Vanka-Vstanka, which wobbles backwards and forwards but always remains erect.
"They won't be forced to ask for a condom, they can ask for a Vanka-Vstanka. It brings in a joke element," said Korotonozhkin. "It gets rid of the customer's psychological barrier.
"We started producing them last year, but we've only been trading them a month. We've sold about a million.

World AIDS Day this weekened will be a low-key event in Russia, although officials and experts say the country -- shielded in the past by communist isolation and state controls -- faces an epidemic of the disease.
Health ministry officials say funds for preventative campaigning have not been forthcoming from the government. This is where the private manufacturers step in.

"Whereas in the West there is direct advertisment, here we have to mask it through anti-AIDS, sexual education programmes," Korotonozhkin said. "The further from Moscow, the worse the attitude to condoms."
